The core argument of the article centers on the moral justification of the lawyer's traditional role as a loyal advocate for their client. Charles Fried challenges the notion that this loyalty to the client is inherently incompatible with moral principles, particularly in contrast to utilitarian critiques that view such loyalty as selfish or harmful to the broader good. He frames the lawyer's role as analogous to the relationship of friendship, where one's commitment to a friend's interests is a morally valid and even essential aspect of that relationship. This analogy is used to justify the lawyer's duty to prioritize their client's needs within the bounds of the law, even when such actions may not align with the interests of society as a whole.
